subject: Help applying Matt Trick to Gelman and Hill (2003) stan example: Chapter 17.2

messages.author: 7e23fa2bc34b1540
messages.subject: Help applying Matt Trick to Gelman and Hill (2003) stan example: Chapter 17.2
parts:
Hello,

I've been working to get up to speed with Stan (using rstan) and I'm wondering if I could get some advice about optimizing code to achieve higher "n_eff" (or Rhat = 1.0) in a shorter amount of time. I'm using some code that was translated from BUGS to stan as a template for my model, specifically an example from Gelman and Hill (2003) Chapter 17.2. If you're not familiar with these examples, it's a varying intercept, varying slope model with correlated parameters written in matrix form.

Would anyone be willing to check my application of the advice for the Matt trick (from the FAQ, as described by Ben Goodrich on 10-11-12) to this example model?

Here is the original code translated by others in this group from the Gelman book and distributed as "unifcorr_mat.g.stan" (Thank you for doing these translations!):


data {
    int<lower=0> N;
    int<lower=0> J;
    int<lower=0> K;
    vector[N] y;
    matrix<lower=0, upper=1>[N,K] X;
    int county[N];
}
parameters {
    vector[K] B[J];
    vector[K] mu_B;
    vector<lower=0>[K] sigma_B;
    corr_matrix[K] R;
    real<lower=0> sigma_y;
}
transformed parameters {
    cov_matrix[K] Sigma_B;
    matrix[K,K] D;
    D <- diag_matrix(sigma_B);
    Sigma_B <- D * R * D;
}
model {
    for (j in 1:J)
        B[j] ~ multi_normal(mu_B, Sigma_B);
    for (n in 1:N)
        y[n] ~ normal(dot_product(B[county[n]], X[n]), sigma_y);
}


Now the code that I have modified to try to apply the Matt Trick using a mean vector zero and correlation matrix R, as described in the FAQ. I've commented out lines that I removed, and added lines are in red text. Sorry for the mess!

'
data {
    int<lower=0> N;
    int<lower=0> J;
    int<lower=0> K;
    vector[N] y;
    matrix<lower=0, upper=1>[N,K] X;
    int county[N];
}
transformed data {
  vector[K] zero_vector;
  for (k in 1:K) {
    zero_vector[k] <- 0;
  }
}
parameters {
    //vector[K] B[J];
    vector[K] e_B[J];
    vector[K] mu_B;
    //vector<lower=0>[K] sigma_B;
    corr_matrix[K] R;
    real<lower=0> tau[K]; //standard deviations
    real<lower=0> sigma_y;
}
transformed parameters {
    //cov_matrix[K] Sigma_B;
    //matrix[K,K] D;
    //D <- diag_matrix(sigma_B);
    //Sigma_B <- D * R * D;
    vector[K] B[J];
    for (k in 1:K) {
      for (j in 1:J) {
          B[j,k] <- mu_B[k] + e_B[j,k] * tau[k];
      }
   }
}
model {
    mu_B ~ normal(0,100);
    tau ~ uniform(0,100);
    //for (j in 1:J)
        //B[j] ~ multi_normal(mu_B, Sigma_B);
    for (j in 1:J)
        e_B[j] ~ normal(zero_vector, R);
    for (n in 1:N)
        y[n] ~ normal(dot_product(B[county[n]], X[n]), sigma_y);
}
'

When I run this modified version, n_eff does go up for a given number of iterations, I'm just not sure I'm applying the trick correctly. Any advice for optimizing this code? I'm new to stan and relatively new to Bayesian models as well, but very happy to find a program that can fit the models I desire to messy ecological data.

One other question, does creating the intermediate matrix "D" in this fragment (below) somehow speed up the code?

transformed parameters {
    cov_matrix[K] Sigma_B;
    matrix[K,K] D;
    D <- diag_matrix(sigma_B);
    Sigma_B <- D * R * D;

Or would the shorter version below (removing the matrix D) behave the same and run at the same speed?

transformed parameters {
    cov_matrix[K] Sigma_B;
    Sigma_B <- diag_matrix(sigma_B) * R * diag_matrix(sigma_B);


I appreciate your help,

Jane

The redone version looks OK in terms of how it's treating B, but it
doesn't look like an exact translation of the first approach because
in the first approach, there's no prior at all on mu_b.

If you really need help here, Ben's the one to ask.

It doesn't look to me like the second version will compile because
R is a matrix and you use normal().

>
> When I run this modified version, n_eff does go up for a given number of iterations, I'm just not sure I'm applying the trick correctly.

Are they giving you the same results in terms of posterior means
and intervals? That's not a 100% guarantee you've done it right,
but a strong indication.

> Any advice for optimizing this code? I'm new to stan and relatively new to Bayesian models as well, but very happy to find a program that can fit the models I desire to messy ecological data.
>
> One other question, does creating the intermediate matrix "D" in this fragment (below) somehow speed up the code?
>
> transformed parameters {
> cov_matrix[K] Sigma_B;
> matrix[K,K] D;
> D <- diag_matrix(sigma_B);
> Sigma_B <- D * R * D;
>
> Or would the shorter version below (removing the matrix D) behave the same and run at the same speed?
>
> transformed parameters {
> cov_matrix[K] Sigma_B;
> Sigma_B <- diag_matrix(sigma_B) * R * diag_matrix(sigma_B);
>

Until the quad_form_diagonal() function comes out in the next release,
the best option is as described in the current manual (but apparently
not in the examples, because the functions weren't there when the examples
were written):

Sigma_B <- diag_pre_multiply(sigma_B,diag_post_multiply(R,sigma_B));

- Bob

messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: Re: Help applying Matt Trick to Gelman and Hill (2003) stan example: Chapter 17.2
parts:
On Friday, March 21, 2014 10:46:48 AM UTC-4, Jane Foster wrote:
Now the code that I have modified to try to apply the Matt Trick using a mean vector zero and correlation matrix R, as described in the FAQ. I've commented out lines that I removed, and added lines are in red text. Sorry for the mess!

I think you have substituted the univariate Matt trick (which presumes a diagonal covariance matrix) for a model with a dense covariance matrix,  where the multivariate Matt trick would be appropriate. And there are some other things you could do as well that would help. I think your .stan file should be

data {
    int<lower=0> N;
    int<lower=0> J;
    int<lower=0> K;
    vector[N] y;
    matrix<lower=0, upper=1>[N,K] X;
    int county[N];
}
parameters {

vector[K] e_B[J];
    vector[K] mu_B;

corr_matrix[K] R;
    vector<lower=0,upper=100>[K] tau //standard deviations

real<lower=0> sigma_y;
}
transformed parameters {

vector[K] B[J];
   {
       matrix[K,K] L;
       L <- diag_matrix(tau) * cholesky_decompose(R);
       for (j in 1:J) B[j] <- mu_B + L * e_B[j];
   }
}
model {
    vector[N] mu_y;
    mu_B ~ normal(0,100);
    //implicit: R ~ lkj_corr(1);
    //implicit: tau ~ uniform(0,100);
    //implicit: sigma_y is positive but improper
    
    //implies B[j] ~ multi_normal(mu_B, diag_matrix(tau) * R * diag_matrix(tau)   
    for (j in 1:J) e_B[j] ~ normal(0, 1);
    for (n in 1:N) mu_y[n] <- dot_product(B[county[n]], X[n]);
    y ~ normal(mu_y, sigma_y);
}

It would be better still to use the onion method that I posted on a couple of other threads so as to avoid taking the Cholesky decomposition of R, but one step at a time.

Ben

Hi Bob and Ben,

Thank you for your responses. I'm still digesting your suggestions, but I'm thankful to have these corrections to work with.

To Bob,

"It doesn't look to me like the second version will compile because
R is a matrix and you use normal()."

You're right. This didn't work unless I changed the distribution in this line to normal(0,1), which was one reason I didn't feel I was implementing the Matt Trick correctly. And thanks for the (current) better formulation for  Sigma_B.

"Sigma_B <- diag_pre_multiply(sigma_B,
               diag_post_multiply(R,sigma_B));"

Ben, your version does give parameter means that better match the original version then my modified code. I'm still working to understand the changes, but I'll get there! I'll try to implement the onion method next. This is a huge help.

Thank you both,
Jane
